opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot. I think the starting point is recognizing that a lot of our current evaluation practice grew out of a benchmark culture, where the goal was to have one fixed dataset, one leaderboard, and a single number that tells you which model is "best." That served the field really well for a while, but it implicitly assumes that there's a context-free notion of quality. Once these models are deployed in hospitals, in classrooms, in customer service, in legal settings, that assumption breaks down pretty quickly. What counts as a good answer depends on who's asking, what they're going to do with it, and what the cost of an error is.

So the way I'd frame it is that evaluation should be thought of less as measuring a property of the model in isolation and more as measuring a property of the model in a deployment. That has a few implications. One is that we need to be much more explicit about the construct we're trying to measure. If someone says a model is "safe" or "helpful" or "fair," we should ask: safe for whom, helpful at what task, fair with respect to which groups and which harms? A lot of my work, and work with collaborators, has been borrowing ideas from measurement theory and psychometrics, things like construct validity, to make that link between the benchmark and the real-world claim more rigorous.

A second implication is that the people who actually use these systems need to be part of defining the evaluation. Domain experts, clinicians, teachers, affected communities often know which failure modes matter most, and those are frequently not the ones that show up in generic benchmarks. A model can look great on an aggregate medical QA score and still fail in ways that a practicing physician would immediately flag as dangerous.

Third, I think we need to be more comfortable with evaluation being ongoing rather than a one-time certification. Contexts shift, user populations shift, and the models themselves get updated. So you want monitoring, you want ways to detect distribution shift, and you want feedback loops from real usage back into the evaluation.

And then finally, there's a practical tension here, because context-specific evaluation is expensive. You can't hand-build a new benchmark for every deployment. So a lot of the interesting research questions are about efficiency: how do you adaptively choose which test items are most informative, how do you reuse evaluation data across related contexts, how do you get reliable conclusions with fewer examples? Ideas like item response theory, adaptive testing, and careful statistical modeling of uncertainty can help a lot there. The goal is to get evaluations that are both grounded in the actual use case and still affordable enough that people will run them.

r001.rationale: It recommends adaptively choosing informative test items, but does not propose selecting context-relevant subsets from a large suite of tests.

r002.rationale: It mentions medical settings and clinicians, but not competing priorities among medical specialties.

r003.rationale: It frames evaluation around deployment context but does not raise how specifically evaluation should target a domain, institution, or individual clinician.

r004.rationale: It discusses adaptive testing, but does not ask whether test subsets could be selected semi-automatically based on an individual's values.

r005.rationale: It says there is no context-free notion of quality and that what counts as a good answer depends on the user, task, and error costs, identifying ambiguity in practical relevance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that most of what we call evaluation today is pretty disconnected from how these models actually get used, and I've come to believe that gap is the central problem in the field right now.

The way I like to frame it is that a benchmark is really a proxy. It's a measurement instrument that stands in for something we actually care about, which is: will this model do the thing this person needs, in this setting, without causing harm? And the moment you say it that way, you realize that the "thing," the "person," and the "setting" are all variables. A model that's great for a clinician triaging patient notes may be terrible for a high school student doing homework, not because the model changed but because what counts as a good answer changed. The tolerance for hedging, the cost of a confident mistake, the baseline knowledge of the user, all of that is context.

So my first point is that evaluations need to be built with a theory of the deployment in mind. Who's using it, what decision are they making, what does failure cost them. That sounds obvious, but if you look at the leaderboards, almost none of that is encoded. We have one number, and people treat it like a universal quality score. I'd compare it to measuring a car by top speed. It's not wrong, it's just not the thing you care about if you're buying a school bus.

The second piece is that context changes what "correct" even means. A lot of our benchmarks have a single gold answer, and that works for arithmetic. But for most real use, there's a distribution of acceptable responses, and which ones are acceptable depends on norms that vary across communities, professions, cultures, languages. Something we've spent a lot of time on in my group is this question of pluralism in evaluation. If you aggregate everyone's preferences into one score, you quietly optimize for the majority or for whoever labeled the data, and you lose the ability to even see that a model is failing some population badly. So contextual evaluation partly means disaggregating, asking "for whom" and "under what norms," rather than reporting an average.

Third, I think we have to take measurement validity seriously, in the social-science sense. In psychometrics there's this whole literature on whether a test actually measures the construct you claim, whether it generalizes, whether it's reliable across repeated administration. ML borrowed the vocabulary of "testing" but very little of the discipline. So when a model scores ninety percent on some reasoning benchmark, what's the construct? Does that transfer to the reasoning a lawyer needs, or a scientist? Usually we don't know, and often the answer turns out to be no. Contextual adaptation means doing the work to validate that your instrument predicts outcomes in the actual setting, which is tedious, but it's the only way the number means anything.

And then the last thing I'd say is that context is dynamic. The model is in a loop with the user. People adapt to it, they learn to prompt it, they over-trust it or under-trust it. So static evaluation is always a snapshot of a system that's moving. I'm increasingly interested in things like interactive evaluation, evaluations with real users in the loop, and post-deployment monitoring that treats the benchmark as the start of the story rather than the end.

If I had to compress all that: stop asking "how good is this model" and start asking "good for what, for whom, and how would we know." That reframing changes almost everything about how you'd design the evaluation.

r003.rationale: It asks who uses a model and in what setting, but does not ask whether evaluation should target a domain, institution, or individual clinician.

r004.rationale: It discusses pluralism and user context, but does not propose semi-automatically selecting tests according to an individual’s values.

r005.rationale: It describes benchmarks as proxies for practical outcomes and says the relevant task, user, and setting are variables, making practical relevance context-dependent.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to ask what people are actually trying to do with the model. A benchmark can tell you something about a capability, but that’s different from telling you whether the model is useful in a particular setting.

For example, if you’re using it to brainstorm, you might value variety and be perfectly happy to discard a few bad suggestions. If you’re using it to help answer a medical question, the consequences of an incorrect answer are very different. So the evaluation needs to reflect the task, the people using the system, and the cost of different kinds of mistakes.

And often the right thing to evaluate is the whole interaction. Does the person, with the model’s assistance, make a better decision? Can they recognize when it’s wrong? Does the model ask for clarification when it doesn’t have enough information? Those things aren’t necessarily captured by scoring a single response against a reference.

So I’d like to see broad benchmarks complemented by evaluations that are much closer to actual use, with feedback from the people in that setting. That gives us a more meaningful answer to the question: useful for whom, and for what?

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to start with what people are actually trying to do. A model can perform very well on a general benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it’s useful for a particular person, in a particular setting.

So, if you’re using a language model to help write code, you care about whether the code works and whether you can maintain it. If you’re using it to help answer medical questions, the kinds of errors you care about, and the consequences of those errors, are quite different. Even within those settings, different users may need different things.

That means evaluating the model as part of a system, including how people interact with it. Do they recognize when it makes a mistake? Does it help them make better decisions, or do they become overconfident? Those questions aren’t captured particularly well by a single accuracy number.

I still think general benchmarks are useful. But we need to connect them to evaluations that reflect the actual task, the users, and the cost of getting things wrong. And that evaluation has to continue as the way people use the system changes.
